name: Intralesional steroid / 5-FU for keloids

lead: Keloids are raised scars that grow beyond the original wound. One long-standing medical approach is to inject a corticosteroid such as triamcinolone directly into the scar, sometimes mixed with the chemotherapy drug 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), to reduce its bulk, itch and redness.

It is a clinical procedure, not a cosmetic product. Wikipedia notes that corticosteroid injections were introduced in the mid-1960s and are used within broader treatment plans that may include laser, cryotherapy or surgery.

paras: Corticosteroids are described as reducing fibroblast activity, inflammation and itching in the scar tissue. 5-FU is an antimetabolite that is used in combination regimens, including a described 'triple therapy' with pulsed dye laser.

Keloids frequently return after treatment, and Wikipedia reports that surgical removal alone has high recurrence. Intralesional corticosteroids are not recommended in children because of possible growth abnormalities. Rare allergic-type reactions have been reported after keloid injections. Injections are given by clinicians; this article gives no instructions.

lead: Intralesional corticosteroid and 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) injection for keloids is a dermatological procedure in which a clinician injects medication directly into a raised keloid scar to reduce its height, firmness and symptoms such as itch. Triamcinolone acetonide is the corticosteroid most commonly named, and 5-FU is sometimes added or used as an alternative [1].

Keloids are benign overgrowths of scar tissue that can extend beyond the boundaries of the original wound. Wikipedia describes corticosteroid injection as appearing to reduce fibroblast activity, inflammation and itching, and notes that it is not recommended for children because of possible growth abnormalities. It also describes a combined 'triple therapy' of corticosteroid, 5-FU and pulsed dye laser, said to enhance results and reduce side effects [1].

Published comparative evidence is limited. Several small registered trials have compared triamcinolone alone with combinations or alternatives such as metformin, bleomycin, botulinum toxin and laser-assisted delivery, many of them with small enrolments [2][3][4][5]. In looksmaxxing communities the topic appears mainly as a medical option for visible scars rather than a self-administered practice.

paras: A keloid is a firm, raised scar that grows past the edges of the original injury and can be itchy or painful. Treatment is usually multimodal, and Wikipedia lists corticosteroid injection, cryotherapy, laser, pressure therapy, silicone sheeting, radiation and surgery among the options [1].

Intralesional corticosteroid injection places the drug within the scar tissue itself. 5-FU, a drug also used in oncology and in other skin conditions, is described as part of combination approaches [1].

Wikipedia states that corticosteroid injection appears to reduce fibroblast activity, inflammation and itch, but provides no pooled recurrence figures for injections [1]. It reports that excision alone has a recurrence rate of 70 to 100 percent and can produce larger lesions, and that combining surgery with other therapies such as radiation, pressure or laser substantially lowers recurrence [1].

A 2022 Cochrane review of silicone gel sheeting compared it with triamcinolone injections among other options but found only two small studies totalling 36 participants, so it could not determine which treatment performs best [1].

Wikipedia notes corticosteroid injection is not recommended in children because of possible growth abnormalities [1]. A French case report described a patient who developed a Hoigne's syndrome reaction, with fear of dying, after an intra-keloid injection of triamcinolone acetonide with lidocaine [6]. Other recognised effects of injected corticosteroids in general, such as local skin changes, are not detailed in the sources reviewed here.

Registered studies of keloid injection treatments include a phase 3 trial of intralesional treatments (NCT06729840, 45 participants, recruiting) [7], a small comparison of post-surgical injection with triamcinolone versus triamcinolone plus fluorouracil (NCT04710719, 7 participants, completed) [2], a phase 2 comparison of intralesional metformin with triamcinolone (NCT07922616, 30 participants, completed) [3], a trial of bleomycin jet injections (NCT04582305, 14 participants) [4], a study of botulinum toxin to prevent keloid recurrence (NCT05072821, 28 participants) [5], a trial of thermo-mechanical fractional ablation to aid triamcinolone delivery (NCT04597060, 25 participants) [8], and a comparison of corticosteroid injection alone versus combined with Nd:YAG or erbium laser (NCT07263100, 20 participants) [9]. Results are not summarised in the registry entries available to this wiki, and the enrolments are small.

Keloid injections are generally discussed as a clinician-delivered treatment for visible scarring, for example on the ear or face, within hardmaxxing-style conversations about improving appearance through medical procedures. No community material on this topic is cited here.

timeline.event: Intralesional corticosteroid injections introduced for keloids and hypertrophic scars. [1]
Pressure therapy begins to be used for scars. [1]
Cochrane reviews of silicone sheeting and laser therapy find limited evidence for comparing treatments. [1]
